ai.definition: A neural firewall is a cybersecurity technology designed to protect brain-computer interface (BCI) systems by preventing unauthorized access to the user's thoughts and cognitive processes.
ai.howItWorks: The neural firewall operates at the biometric hash-filter level, creating a barrier between the BCI hardware and the user’s neural signals. It uses advanced encryption techniques to authenticate the user and filter out any unauthorized attempts to intercept or manipulate these signals.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the security risks associated with BCIs, such as unauthorized access, data breaches, and potential manipulation of a user's thoughts and actions.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing biometric hash-filtering algorithms, integrating them into BCI devices, and ensuring secure communication channels between the hardware and software components.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing and testing the biometric filters, implementing encryption protocols, and creating a seamless integration with existing BCI systems. This requires collaboration between cybersecurity experts, neuroscientists, and engineers.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development of advanced biometric algorithms, high-quality hardware for secure communication, and rigorous testing to ensure reliability and security.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is in its early stages, with significant potential but facing challenges in practical implementation and regulatory approval.
ai.regulation: There are currently no specific regulations governing neural firewalls, but they will likely face scrutiny from privacy and security regulators as the technology advances.
ai.risks: Risks include technical limitations in biometric filtering, potential vulnerabilities in encryption protocols, and ethical concerns related to thought privacy.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain at this stage due to the high research and development costs and the need for extensive testing and validation before commercialization.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving biometric accuracy, enhancing security features, and addressing regulatory and ethical concerns.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking.

glossary.def: Brain-Computer Interface, a system that enables direct communication between the brain and external devices.
A method of authentication and data protection using biometric signals to create unique hashes for secure access.

subsystems.name: Neural interface
subsystems.role: the electrode array and electronics that read neural activity — and, in a few devices, write it back by stimulation.
parts: penetrating microelectrode array or surface electrode grid

subsystems.name: Hardware root of trust
subsystems.role: a tamper-resistant chip that stores keys and proves the implant is genuine.
parts: secure element or physically unclonable function

subsystems.name: Neural signature module
subsystems.role: derives a stable, individual identifier from the user's own brain activity patterns.
parts: matcher with tolerance for natural drift

subsystems.name: Link security layer
subsystems.role: encrypts and authenticates everything crossing the skin.

subsystems.name: Command mediation engine
subsystems.role: decides which decoded intentions may become actions, and blocks the rest.
parts: policy rules for read, write and stimulation commands

subsystems.name: Anomaly monitor
subsystems.role: flags activity that does not look like the user's normal patterns or the device's normal behaviour.

subsystems.name: Audit and consent layer
subsystems.role: keeps privacy-preserving records of access and gives the user control over them.

buildSteps.title: Model the threat
buildSteps.detail: List what an attacker could do: read decoded thoughts, inject stimulation, replay a recorded session, relay a remote attacker into the link via a nearby phone, or simply drain the battery to force a reboot into an unsafe state.

buildSteps.title: Characterise the user's neural baseline
buildSteps.detail: Record resting and task activity over weeks so the system knows what is normal for this person and how much it drifts with sleep, medication and time.

buildSteps.title: Build the identity primitive
buildSteps.detail: Extract features that are stable and hard to copy from someone else's recordings, then turn them into a key or verification score rather than storing raw brain data.

buildSteps.title: Put trust in hardware
buildSteps.detail: Add a secure element that holds keys, measures the device's own state, and refuses to transmit if the enclosure, supply voltage or clock looks tampered with.

buildSteps.title: Secure the wireless link
buildSteps.detail: Adapt proven lightweight cryptography — the kind used for constrained radios — so that encryption, authentication and replay protection fit inside a milliwatt and a few kilobits per second.

buildSteps.title: Insert the mediation layer
buildSteps.detail: Place a policy engine between the decoder and any actuator or external device: it checks identity, command type, rate and stimulation limits before anything is executed.

buildSteps.title: Train the anomaly monitor
buildSteps.detail: Teach a detector on the user's own data to spot injected signals, unusual command sequences or a second party on the link, and to cut the session when it is unsure.

buildSteps.title: Adversarially test the whole stack
buildSteps.detail: Red-team with magnet fields, radio jamming, spoofed pairing devices and recorded-signal replay, first in animals and then in implanted volunteers, under ethics and regulatory oversight.

buildSteps.title: Plan updates and failure
buildSteps.detail: Provide signed firmware updates, key revocation, and a documented behaviour for when the implant fails — the default must be to stop, not to keep stimulating.

prerequisites.why: high-channel recording exists in research and limited clinical use, but reliable, safe writing of information back into neural tissue is far less mature.

prerequisites.tech: Neural decoding good enough to define a command
prerequisites.why: you can only firewall an intention if the system can turn it into an explicit, checkable action such as 'send message'.

prerequisites.tech: Secure low-power computing on an implant
prerequisites.why: cryptography and anomaly detection must run on a device with a tiny power and heat budget inside the body.
a 2012 study showed a consumer EEG headset could be used to infer sensitive information such as PINs, so the attack surface is real but only partly mapped.

prerequisites.tech: Rules for neural data privacy and device security
prerequisites.why: without agreed standards for access, consent and breach reporting, a firewall has nothing to enforce.

pathway.milestone: academic attacks and defences demonstrated on EEG headsets and research implants
pathway.unlocks: a shared vocabulary of neural privacy threats.

pathway.milestone: authenticated, encrypted links inside clinical implants such as hearing and motor prostheses
pathway.unlocks: regulators and manufacturers treating neurodata like other sensitive medical data.

pathway.milestone: a proven neural-signature or user-verification method that survives daily drift
pathway.unlocks: continuous identity checks without a password or a phone.

pathway.milestone: a co-designed security architecture shipped with consumer-grade implanted devices
pathway.unlocks: using a BCI for payments, messages or control of equipment without handing an attacker a direct line to the brain.
